clue.text: Tail of Flying Fortress initially eliminated as cause of trouble for airmen

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its final letter, here taken from the word Flying
the opening letter of the fortress word is removed, as initially says it is the first to go

parts.note: a kremlin is a citadel or fortress, as in the Moscow Kremlin

explanation.surface: A wartime bomber loses its tail section, putting the crew in danger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flying Fortress' reads as the B-17 bomber, but the two words split: the tail of Flying, then the Moscow citadel word with its first letter removed.
explanation.definitionFit: In RAF folklore a mischievous imp was blamed for unexplained mechanical faults in aircraft.

clue.text: Rabbit pie's very good, served up without starter in eatery

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means the pieces read upwards, so the letters are reversed
without signals removing a letter from the pie word

parts.note: pie's gives the letters PIES once the apostrophe is dropped

indicators.note: the starter is the first letter of the word eatery

parts.note: so means very, as in so good

explanation.surface: A diner's pie tastes very good when it arrives with no first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit' means chatter, as in British 'rabbit on'. Take E (first letter of eatery) out of PIES, add SO and G, and 'served up' turns PISSOG upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To rabbit on is to talk at length, so the definition means chat idly or tattle.

clue.text: One demands Guinness?

explanation.surface: Someone orders a pint of the famous Irish stout.
explanation.walkthrough: Guinness looks like the stout, but it is Sir Alec Guinness, a film actor who died in 2000, so he is an ex-actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who exacts payment insists on it; a late actor such as Alec Guinness is a former player on screen.

clue.text: Old fellows in retirement need first and foremost to get sleep

indicators.note: first and foremost puts the getting word in front of the other pieces

parts.note: to land a prize or job is to get it
F is the abbreviation for fellow

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the college fellow is read backwards

parts.note: a don is a fellow of an Oxford or Cambridge college

explanation.surface: Elderly academics need sleep above all once they have retired.
explanation.walkthrough: One word, 'fellows', gives two fellows: the abbreviation and the college fellow, which 'in retirement' turns round. 'first and foremost' puts the getting word at the front, and 'need' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Land of Nod is a joking name for the state of sleep, from the place where Cain was sent in Genesis.

clue.text: A century back maybe an East London idiom for diddly-squat

indicators.note: back means read in reverse, so the century phrase is turned round

parts.note: a ton is a hundred, so a century is a ton
East London is a port city in South Africa, whose abbreviation is SA
usage is the idiom or customary way a language is used

explanation.surface: A Cockney turn of phrase from a hundred years ago meant nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East London' points to Cockney speech, but it is the city in South Africa, which gives SA. 'maybe' marks it as an example, and 'A century' is A TON, read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The British slang phrase means nothing at all, the same as zilch.

clue.text: Coarse stuff from two males

parts.note: a buck is a male deer or rabbit
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: A rough fabric is made from the wool of two male animals.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says 'two males', so one word supplies both pieces: BUCK, a male deer, and RAM, a male sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: This stiff, rough cloth of linen or cotton is used in bookbinding and for stiffening garments.

clue.text: Friend is to call back

indicators.note: back means the calling word is read in reverse

parts.note: to dub someone is to call or name them

explanation.surface: A friend has to phone someone back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'call back' looks like returning a phone call, but it means turning DUB round. 'is to' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: An American colloquial term for a pal or mate.

clue.text: Apprentice meets a nationalist from island republic

parts.note: a cub is a trainee or apprentice, as in cub reporter

explanation.surface: A young trainee meets a nationalist from a Caribbean island state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apprentice' gives CUB, as in a cub reporter. N for nationalist is a standard abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuba is a Caribbean island state, so its people and products are described this way.

clue.text: Move to new location outside Portugal's capital for a break

indicators.note: outside means the relocating word goes around the initial letter

parts.note: to resite something is to move it to a new site

indicators.note: a capital letter is the first, so the opening letter of Portugal's is taken

explanation.surface: Someone moves away from Lisbon to take a holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Portugal's capital' suggests Lisbon, but it means P, the first letter of Portugal. 'outside' puts RESITE around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A respite is a short rest or pause from something hard or unpleasant.

clue.text: Fancy sandwiches available reflected price of bread

indicators.note: sandwiches means the exclamation word holds the other pieces between its letters

parts.note: Fancy! and My! are both exclamations of surprise
on means available, as in beer on tap

indicators.note: reflected means mirrored, so the price word is read backwards

parts.note: a rate is a price or charge

explanation.surface: Posh sandwiches cost as much as a loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy sandwiches' reads as posh food, but Fancy is an exclamation of surprise. It holds the available word, then the price word turned round by 'reflected'. 'bread' is slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread is slang for money, so the definition means to do with cash or currency.

clue.text: Obtaining a low grade, failed test and made no progress

indicators.note: obtaining here means getting hold of, so the jumbled letters take the other pieces into their middle
something that has failed has fallen apart, so the letters of the words test and and are rearranged

parts.note: G is the lowest pass grade on some exam scales, such as the old British GCSE

explanation.surface: A student scrapes a poor mark, flunks an exam and gets nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' looks like a joining word but is part of the anagram that 'failed' signals. 'Obtaining' puts A and the low grade inside the rearranged letters, after their first two.
explanation.definitionFit: Water or an economy that stagnates stays still and shows no growth or development.

clue.text: Ship's officer's perk — that's exchanging partners

indicators.note: in bridge North and South are partners, so the letters N and S swap places in the word

parts.note: a bonus is an extra perk on top of pay

explanation.surface: A naval officer's fringe benefit involves wife-swapping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exchanging partners' suggests swinging, but the partners are N and S, North and South at the bridge table. Swap them in BONUS to get the ship's officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A boatswain, shortened in speech and spelling, is the ship's petty officer in charge of rigging and deck crew.

clue.text: Opening bars? It's essential to restrain troublemakers

indicators.note: It's essential to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Keeping rowdy people in check is the key to stopping a pub fight early.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening bars' suggests pubs opening their doors, but it means the first bars of music. The letters sit inside restraIN TROublemakers.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of music begins with a short introductory passage before the main tune.

clue.text: Born perhaps as result of incest — it's shocking

indicators.note: shocking hints at something knocked out of shape, so the letters of incest and it's are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is said to exist only because of a scandalous family union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Born' looks like a verb about birth, but it is Max Born, the German-British physicist. 'as result of' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Born won the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on quantum mechanics, so he is one example of a researcher.

clue.text: Violetta or Alfred's heart broken in this opera?

indicators.note: broken means smashed apart, so the letters are rearranged
the heart of a word is its middle letter, here the middle of Alfred's

explanation.surface: Two lovers from Verdi have their hearts broken in an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Violetta and Alfredo are lovers in Verdi's La Traviata, not in this opera, so the question mark is a tease. R is the middle letter of ALFREDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's 1853 opera about a troubadour is one example of a music drama.

clue.text: Be last to get raises, having introduced most of them

indicators.note: having introduced means the two raising words take another piece in between them

parts.note: to bring up children is to raise them
to rear children is also to raise them

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter, so the final letter of them goes

explanation.surface: Someone gets pay rises only after introducing most of the colleagues around them.
explanation.walkthrough: One word, 'raises', gives two synonyms, and 'having introduced' puts the shortened third piece between them; 'most of' means the last letter goes. 'to get' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who brings up the rear comes at the end of a procession or finishes after everyone else.

clue.text: He tucked into Mum's pie, high in sugar?

indicators.note: tucked into means the pronoun is placed inside the jumbled letters
high means gone off, like meat, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: Mum's gives the letters MUMS once the apostrophe is dropped

explanation.surface: A man gobbles his mother's pie and is buzzing from all the sugar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucked into' reads as eating, but it puts the pronoun inside the letters of Mum's pie, rearranged by 'high' (gone off, like meat). 'Sugar!' is said in place of a ruder word.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying sugar in place of a swear word is a mild stand-in for a harsher term.

clue.text: Dad's up himself? That's obvious

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the dad word reads upwards, so its letters are reversed

parts.note: Pa is a familiar word for father
himself refers back to Dad, who is a parent

explanation.surface: Dad is full of himself, and everyone can see it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up himself' looks like British slang for conceited, but 'up' turns the dad word round and 'himself' refers back to Dad.
explanation.definitionFit: Something apparent is plain to see or evident.

clue.text: Ah, padre! Clue to that is difficult relationship with step-parent

parts.note: read the answer as wordplay: the name in it is a jumble of these letters, and its second word is the signal for that jumble

explanation.surface: Someone calls on a priest for help with a tricky family puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read the answer as a clue, and the second word, meaning intricate, rearranges the first. That gives the letters of AH PADRE, which is why the clue says 'Clue to that'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Phaedra fell in love with her stepson Hippolytus, so the term names a desire for a step-parent or stepchild.

clue.text: One reviewing books needs a university degree? Rubbish, I retorted

indicators.note: retorted is read as turned back, so the words Rubbish and I are read backwards together

parts.note: rot means rubbish or nonsense

explanation.surface: Someone says a reviewer needs a university degree, and gets the reply that this is nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'books' means accounts, not novels, and 'Rubbish, I retorted' is not a reply: 'retorted' turns round the rubbish word together with I.
explanation.definitionFit: An auditor checks a company's financial records, its books, for accuracy.

clue.text: Powerful woman is to go down well with new leadership

indicators.note: leadership is the opening letter, so a different first letter replaces the original

parts.note: to impress is to go down well with someone

explanation.surface: A strong female leader has to win people over with fresh ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new leadership' changes only the first letter: the I of IMPRESS becomes E. 'is to' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman ruling an empire, or the wife of an emperor, holds great power.

clue.text: Happy Hour involves principally booze low in alcohol? On the contrary

indicators.note: principally means the first letter of the word booze
involves means takes in, so one piece sits inside another
On the contrary flips the containment: the drink pieces go around the hour letter, not the reverse

parts.note: lite is a commercial spelling of light, used for low-alcohol drinks

explanation.surface: A bar's happy hour serves mainly weak drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as written, H would hold the other letters. 'On the contrary' swaps that: B plus LITE goes around H.
explanation.definitionFit: Blithe means cheerful and carefree.

clue.text: Some stars protest about appearing in a new play after 40% cut

indicators.note: appearing in says the turned protest goes inside the shortened play
two of five letters is 40%, so the play word keeps only its first three letters

parts.note: a drama is a play

indicators.note: about signals turning round, so the protest word is read backwards

parts.note: a demo is a protest march

explanation.surface: A protest breaks out in a new stage play after its budget is cut by 40%.
explanation.walkthrough: 'play' is DRAMA, and 'after 40% cut' drops two of its five letters. 'about' turns the protest round, and 'appearing in' puts it inside what is left of the play, after A and N (new).
explanation.definitionFit: This northern constellation, named after the princess chained to a rock in Greek myth, is a group of stars.

clue.text: Worked hard with no time wasted

indicators.note: with no means the time letter is removed from the word

parts.note: to toil is to work hard

explanation.surface: Someone worked hard and wasted no time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wasted' looks like part of 'no time wasted', but it is the definition: slang for drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-oiled is British slang for drunk, as is wasted.

clue.text: Throw out appeals regularly, having examined precedent

indicators.note: precedent means coming before, so the examined abbreviation goes in front

parts.note: ex. is a dictionary abbreviation for examined

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the word appeals

explanation.surface: A court rejects appeals as a matter of routine after looking at case law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'precedent' looks like legal jargon, but it is a position word: the examined abbreviation comes first, then the alternate letters of appeals.
explanation.definitionFit: To eject someone or something is to force them out, as a school does a pupil.

clue.text: Review of books by European's the first to lavish praise

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for European
by gives X, as in 3 by 4 for multiplication

indicators.note: review read as re-view, looking back, so the books abbreviation is turned around

parts.note: OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible

indicators.note: the first letter of the word lavish is taken

explanation.surface: A European writes a review of books and is the first to heap praise on them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Review' looks like a book review, but it means looking back, so the books abbreviation is turned round. 'by' is the multiplication sign, and 'lavish' gives only its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol something is to praise it highly and enthusiastically.

clue.text: Cautious driver, in the main, on rum — in pints!

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the pints abbreviation

parts.note: PT is the abbreviation for pint

indicators.note: rum means odd or strange, so the letters are rearranged
in the main means mostly, so the word driver loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A motorist who has drunk rum by the pint calls himself careful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the main' suggests the sea but means mostly, so driver loses its last letter. 'rum' rearranges that with ON, and 'in' puts the result inside the pints abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A provident person plans ahead and saves for the future, so is careful with money.

clue.text: Press misses heart of the matter

indicators.note: misses means goes without, so a letter is removed from the press word

parts.note: to push is to press

indicators.note: the heart is the middle letter of the word the

explanation.surface: The newspapers fail to grasp what a story is really about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heart of the matter' reads as one phrase, but it splits: H, the middle of 'the', is lost from PUSH, and 'matter' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pus is the yellowish fluid that forms in an infected wound, a kind of bodily discharge.

clue.text: One stops exchanges becoming torrents of abuse

indicators.note: stops is read as plugs, so one letter sits inside the other word like a stopper

parts.note: trades are exchanges of goods
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: One person calls a halt to arguments that are turning into shouting matches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stops' reads as ends, but it means fills a hole: I sits inside TRADES. 'becoming' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: A long, angry speech of denunciation is a rant or harangue.

clue.text: As one's awfully mean, small tips for waiters ensue

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so the letters of mean are rearranged

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

indicators.note: tips are the first letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Because one customer is so stingy, tiny tips for the waiting staff follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tips' suggests gratuities, but it means the first letters of waiters and ensue. 'awfully' rearranges MEAN into ENMA.
explanation.definitionFit: A French phrase meaning all together, in a body, as a group.
